clue.text: In the morning, gripped compass

parts.note: am = ante meridiem, before noon
bit = gripped with the teeth

explanation.surface: A hiker grabs their compass first thing in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compass' is the magnetic instrument in the surface, but here it means range or scope, the sense of 'within the compass of'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambit is the scope or extent of something, which is what a compass means in 'beyond my compass'.

clue.text: Nearly missing over border

indicators.note: the word is lacking the next item, so it is taken out

parts.note: about = nearly, as in 'about ten'
O = over, the cricket abbreviation; it is removed

explanation.surface: A near miss on the frontier line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Border' is a verb here: to abut is to border on something.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that abut each other border each other, sharing an edge.

clue.text: I'm surprised to be embraced by British Nobel laureate

indicators.note: the exclamation is held inside the abbreviation, as if hugged

parts.note: Br = British, the standard abbreviation
oh! = an exclamation of surprise, placed inside BR

explanation.surface: Someone is astonished to be hugged by a British prize winner.
explanation.walkthrough: Niels Bohr was Danish, so 'British' is not part of the definition; it supplies BR and the laureate stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Niels Bohr won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on atomic structure.

clue.text: Italian stronghold in Otranto periodically offers retaliation

indicators.note: the Italian and the stronghold sit inside the letters taken from the town
at regular intervals, so every other letter of Otranto is taken

parts.note: the town of Otranto, whose second, fourth and sixth letters are taken
a fort is a stronghold

explanation.surface: A castle in the southern Italian port of Otranto hands out revenge now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: IT is the usual abbreviation for Italian, as on vermouth labels.
explanation.definitionFit: Tit for tat is an idiom for paying back an injury in kind, which is retaliation.

clue.text: Hated communist encapsulates wickedness

indicators.note: the outer word holds the other inside it like a capsule

parts.note: a red = a communist
vile = wicked; placed inside RE…D

explanation.surface: A loathed communist embodies evil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wickedness' is a noun but gives the adjective VILE; the clue asks for the idea, so solvers accept the loose part of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Reviled means abused and despised, so strongly hated.

clue.text: Hackneyed output on the subject of mess

parts.note: re = concerning, as in a memo heading
to make a hash of something is to make a mess of it

explanation.surface: Tired old writing about some muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: A rehash is old material served up again, hence hackneyed output.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehash is something produced by reworking old material, which is stale, hackneyed output.

clue.text: Energy provider's centre opening in May

indicators.note: the centre of provider is its two middle letters

parts.note: the word provider, its middle taken

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the month name, whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A power company's head office opens in the spring.
explanation.definitionFit: Vim means vigour or liveliness, a lively kind of energy.

clue.text: Mourned for soldiers among deceased 500

indicators.note: one part is placed in the middle of another

parts.note: the late = the deceased
men = soldiers, as in 'officers and men'; placed inside LA…TE
D = 500 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A memorial to five hundred fallen soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a war memorial, so every word seems to belong to the definition; only 'Mourned for' does.
explanation.definitionFit: To lament someone is to mourn them, so lamented means mourned for.

clue.text: Separate record on damaged tree

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A vinyl record has been left lying on a broken tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Separate' could be a verb, but the answer is the adjective, distinct from discreet, which means tactful.
explanation.definitionFit: Discrete means individually distinct, so discrete things are separate from one another.

clue.text: Release one French jerk

parts.note: un = one in French
a hitch is a sudden jerk or tug

explanation.surface: Setting free a French idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' looks like an insult for the Frenchman, but it means a sudden pull, which is a hitch.
explanation.definitionFit: To unhitch a horse or trailer is to release it from what holds it.

clue.text: Notes, a few minutes, sent over

indicators.note: turned over, so written back to front

parts.note: some = a few
m = minutes, the abbreviation

explanation.surface: A few quick notes are dispatched after a couple of minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make 'a few minutes' look like a time delay, but it splits into SOME and M.
explanation.definitionFit: Memos are short written notes passed around an office.

clue.text: Perhaps bone is a mess

definitions.meaning: a bone is an example of what a dog eats
a muddle or botched job; this sense is British slang

explanation.surface: A bone left lying around is untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks a bone as just one example of a dog's dinner. In British slang, making a dog's dinner of something means making a mess of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's dinner is British slang for a mess, and literally a bone could be one.

clue.text: Preface reduction, somehow

indicators.note: in some way or other, so the letters are arranged differently

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: An editor cuts a book's preface down somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preface' is a verb here: to preface a talk is to introduce it.
explanation.definitionFit: To preface something is to introduce it with opening remarks.

clue.text: Criminal studied entrance to prison in question

indicators.note: wrong or bad, so the letters go astray

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: the first letter, the way into the word

parts.note: the first letter of prison, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: A crook who studied is questioned on arriving in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like the person being questioned, but it only tells you to mix up the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter in question is being disputed, argued over and not settled.

clue.text: Make repairs along said passage

parts.note: over = along, as in 'walk over the bridge'

indicators.note: spoken, so the word is what you hear rather than how it is spelt

parts.note: a hall is a passage; HAUL sounds the same in British speech

explanation.surface: A builder fixing things along a narrated corridor.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech, which drops the R, HALL and HAUL sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: To overhaul an engine is to take it apart and repair it thoroughly.

clue.text: Welcome in first of trainees in brief inspection

indicators.note: the trainee's letter sits inside the shortened inspection
cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a view is an inspection, as of a property

indicators.note: the first letter of the word trainees

parts.note: the word trainees, whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: New recruits are greeted as they file in for a quick once-over.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is simply the letters IN; the second places the trainee's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To invite someone is to ask them in, extending a welcome as a host does.

clue.text: Static rates should change with time

indicators.note: the letters are to be altered into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
t = time, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: Frozen interest rates ought to move eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is economics: static rates that need to change over time. 'Static' is the definition, meaning not moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at rest is not moving, which is what static means.

clue.text: Lecherous type lowers large coat

indicators.note: the letter for large is lowered, moved one place further down this down entry

parts.note: a luster is one who lusts
the first two letters of the lecher's word, L for large on top
the same two letters with large lowered beneath the U

explanation.surface: A lecher drops his big overcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large; in LUSTER it slips below the U.
explanation.definitionFit: An ulster is a long loose overcoat, originally made in Belfast, so it is a kind of coat.

clue.text: Welsh town's drunk part blotto

indicators.note: the letters stagger about, out of order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A Welsh town is partly drunk already.
explanation.walkthrough: Port Talbot is a steel town in South Wales. 'Blotto' means very drunk, so 'drunk' and 'blotto' seem to repeat each other; one is the indicator, one is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Port Talbot is an industrial town on the south Wales coast.

clue.text: Joke cigars ultimately wrapped in black

indicators.note: the letter is enclosed by the word for black

parts.note: jet is a deep glossy black

indicators.note: the final letter of the word cigars

parts.note: the word cigars, whose last letter is taken

explanation.surface: Someone's cigars all come rolled in black paper, a gag of sorts.
explanation.definitionFit: A jest is a joke or a playful remark meant to amuse.

clue.text: Starts to take up bronze age instrument

indicators.note: take the starting letter of each following word

parts.note: the first letters of Take Up Bronze Age

explanation.surface: An archaeologist unearths a Bronze Age musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bronze Age sounds like the date of the instrument, but those words are only there for their initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is a large brass wind instrument.

clue.text: Fly back, retaining western accent

indicators.note: the insect holds the letter inside it
a fly flying back travels the other way, so its letters are read right to left

parts.note: a gnat is a small fly
W = western, placed inside GNA…T before the turnaround

explanation.surface: A fly returns, keeping a cowboy accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Western' with 'accent' suggests a cowboy drawl, which a twang is, but in the wordplay it is just W.
explanation.definitionFit: A twang is a nasal accent, like a Texan or Australian twang.

clue.text: Backing essentially saved Hugo Boss

indicators.note: backing means the letters taken are then read in reverse order
essentially means the central letters at the heart of each word

explanation.surface: A fashion house, Hugo Boss, was rescued thanks to financial backing.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of saved is V and of Hugo is UG; VUG reversed gives the answer. 'Hugo Boss' looks like the brand, but Boss is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Guv, short for governor, is informal British slang for a boss or person in charge.

clue.text: Greek character grabs vulgar Canadian Liberal

indicators.note: the outer word takes hold of the other word inside it

parts.note: tau = the Greek letter T
rude = vulgar; placed inside T…AU

explanation.surface: A Greek man seizes a crude Canadian politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Pierre and Justin Trudeau were both Liberal prime ministers of Canada. 'Character' means a letter, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Justin Trudeau, like his father Pierre, led Canada's Liberal Party as prime minister.

clue.text: Present first half of demo standing by organ

indicators.note: standing by means next to, so the organ is placed right after the half-word
first half of takes the opening two of the four letters of demo

parts.note: the liver is a bodily organ

explanation.surface: A demonstrator presents the first part of a demo while standing beside a church organ.
explanation.definitionFit: To present a speech or a parcel is to hand it over or give it out.

clue.text: Additional member of cast doing little

definitions.meaning: more than is usual or expected
a film or stage performer hired to stand in the background

explanation.surface: A bit-part actor with almost nothing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: An extra in a film stands in the background, so does very little.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: the adjective means more than usual, and the film noun is a background performer with no lines.
